Allan Savory is the undisputed international expert on integrated rangeland management . I had been practicing my holistic management approach for 15 years before I heard about Allan Savory. I saw his talk and thought I knew as much about holistic rangeland management as anyone in the world. I heard Allan Savory speak about 5 years ago and almost immediately realized that he knew much more than I did .
Wills Words-

As a result, I began to study his work and eventually made the decision to turn White Oak Pastures into a Savory Center, a center for holistic management. There are 22 or 23 such centers in the world on six continents. There are three east of the Mississippi River, and White Oak Pastures is one of them.
Wills Words-

This means that we study and practice holistic rangeland management. It is primarily about using the influence of animals to shape our land the way we want. The first thing a land manager must do within the framework of holistic management is to determine the context in which he wants to see his land.
Wills Words-

For us, this is a savanna with perennial heat-loving grasses of many species and 20–30% shading. We use animal influence to achieve this. The land we own or acquire usually falls into one of five categories. This is a bit of abandoned land that is very easy to work with. These are planted pine trees that are quite easy to work with, a little more difficult, but quite possible.
Wills Words-

Lowland areas with hardwood trees that can be called swamps. Open pastures, which used to be my farm , or arable land. Arable land is by far the most difficult type of land to work on. The arable land in my region was exhausted to death by the Southern " troika": a crop rotation of corn, cotton, and peanuts.
Wills Words-

Monocultures of corn, cotton and peanuts, alternating with each other. Each of these industrially grown crops depletes the land. Peanuts harm the land due to intensive tillage. They plow the soil deeply, turning it over and destroying all microbial life within. Corn harms the land because of the large amount of chemical fertilizers used.
Wills Words-

They can apply up to 300 pounds of nitrogen fertilizer, which oxidizes any organic matter. And cotton harms the land because it contributes to erosion. The thing is, it just doesn't cover the soil very well. So restoring these lands through animal influence became my passion. We buy or lease these farms adjacent to White Oak Pastures and use the animals there.
Wills Words-

If you take our pigs and goats, they are forest dwellers, and they are great at helping to clear the forest, which otherwise turns into a real jungle, which is what happens on the coastal plain where I live. It gets 52-54 inches of rain a year, it's a semi-tropical climate, so goats and pigs help clear it, and we drive them through until the forest takes on the desired appearance.
Wills Words-

Cows and sheep are grazing animals, and we drive them through different pastures. I like them to move every three days. Three days is a kind of magic for me, because it allows me to get ahead of parasites: roundworms, gastrointestinal nematodes, horn flies, or facial flies. By the time these pests multiply, the cows or sheep will have already moved elsewhere .
Wills Words-

This is very important for the grass itself. Grass grows in an S-shaped curve. So if you let the animals eat it once and drive them away before they bite a second time, the recovery period will be much faster than if they were to constantly graze it, depleting the energy stores in the roots. Stability is not enough. We cannot survive and thrive in the current agricultural situation. We must do better. We need to revive . Our traditional agriculture today is depleting soil fertility . How long can we live until this land becomes unproductive? If we lose the land, it's like losing everything .

I don't think there is a greater task than rejuvenating the soil and improving our health. My name is Walker Keir, and I'm from Pacific Palisades, California. It's easy to look at the livestock here and think that we're just raising them for grass-fed meat that will go to the stores and be sold. They think that's what happens.

But there is a lot going on inside the Earth that we cannot see . So, it's important for people to know that, in addition to raising healthy meat, it's an important part of this equation. The other half is that we are helping the planet at the same time . We are examining the evidence on how grazing on grasslands or arable land can mitigate climate change .

There is a lot of data showing how much carbon can be stored in the soil by growing grass. Because when we send cattle here to graze, as they eat the grass, the plant absorbs carbon from the atmosphere through the process of photosynthesis and releases it into the soil, trying to grow again . Some of that carbon is used for plant growth , but most of it is stored in the soil.

These strategies can add three or four tons of carbon per year to an acre of land. One ton of carbon is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 in the atmosphere. When we talk about storing millions of tons of CO2 to affect climate change , this is a very large amount. It's very easy to say that. To be honest , it's not that easy.

You really have to manage it well . The key word in this whole process is that you need to manage this livestock grazing , because rest is very important for the plants to regrow and release carbon into the soil before grazing again. Ultimately, we want to trample a third, graze a third, and leave a third .

If we leave a third, there will be enough plant there to start photosynthesis effectively without taking too much energy from the root system. If we trample down a third, it helps to mulch the soil and lower the soil temperature , and then the plant decomposes into organic matter in the soil . And if we graze a third, naturally, the animals will be full and happy .

Where our farm is located , we fenced off every area that was not suitable for plowing and growing grain crops and turned it into pasture. This is called set grazing , where you have an area , you keep the animals there during the growing season, you don't move them, they eat what's there. That in itself is not very good for the earth.

So, all the old methods are definitely not great . We have patchworked the old pastures in those fields , but we are moving cattle through them . So, they go in at a higher density, spend a day or two on that lawn , and then we move them, let the land rest and let the plants grow back. Meanwhile, the cattle are fertilizing the land .

In the American imagination, family farms still exist as it has for lifetimes. Farmers have been the seeds of American life and they harbor jobs we cannot afford to lose. Jobs that take courage, intelligence, and resilience. But in reality, American farming is in crisis. The system is dominated by industrial corporate agriculture.

That's not the way it used to be. And at Heifer USA, we aim to rewrite the story of American farming. The main purpose of Heifer USA is to train small holder farmers in regenerative agricultural practices and then connect them to reliable markets so that they can earn a profitable income. Heifer offers support to farmers by linking them to the Grassroots Farmers Co-op and the Cypress Valley Meat Company.

Heifer USA recruits and trains the farmers. Grassroots connects those farmers to markets and then Cypress Valley ensures the animals are harvested in a humane way. All three of us are working together to create a food chain of integrity. Processing is a vital role in farming. You need to find a processor that cares for your animal and your product just as much as you did while you had the animal on your farm.

At our processing facility, our values with Heifers are very much aligned. Heifers helped us professionalize our team and professionalize our operations. It's not just a job, it's a it's a career. You know, I'm getting a a living wage and I have an opportunity to better myself in the company. Modern farming faces numerous challenges today and it needs reform.

Currently, the world's soils are heading for depletion with an estimated 60 harvests left before they are too barren to feed the planet. At the ranch, we practice regenerative agriculture. What is that? We work with nature instead of against it. So, every practice we have here at the ranch is thinking about the ecosystem health and soil health and how we can make that better.

We believe the food system needs to change. We want to see food chains of integrity where farmers are getting paid a living wage, the processing employees are getting paid a living wage, and the environment and the animals are being treated fairly. The United States farmers are growing older. The average age of the farmer is 58 years old.

Heifer USA is determined to reintroduce farming culture to a new generation of Americans. So, Heifer's role in addressing the need for new farmers is one through our social media, YouTube and Instagram, and then secondly through our residential volunteer program. People can come here, live on site, or even volunteer for the day or the week to work alongside our farmers and see what farming looks like first hand.

Over the last couple years we've trained about 100,000 farmers, and that's been through on-farm training as well as online training. We value these things. We value the environment. The partnership between Grass Roots, Suffolk Valley, and Heifer USA is to get the highest quality product from pasture to plate.

We are a family farm, we have two units or two estates . We are in Zapatera , which is about 220 hectares , and then there is also Mundos Nuevos , which is about 350 or so . We have sheep , about 13 sheep , and a pig farm . Mundos Nuevos is a farm that we inherited from our father . He had a more traditional management style ; he practiced agriculture , he sowed .

Then he had sheep as well . My brother took over , and things really accelerated with CAP subsidies , and we started sowing the whole farm ; we started to see that the sheep had less and less land to graze . Let's say we adopted the entire technological package of the Green Revolution ; we brought in more powerful machinery , fertilizers , soil analysis , chemical fertilizers , and herbicides .

At first, it went well because we were getting good harvests and good yields , but after 15 or 20 years of this management , we saw that the soil was exhausted , that even though we increased fertilizer and such , the yield was falling , and we were facing a lot of erosion problems , with bare soil .

The intensive agricultural model demonstrates or makes you see that it is incompatible with livestock farming because you are continuously tilling the soil , and the livestock has less and less pasture , especially less permanent pasture . It’s about taking advantage of the stubble , it’s a more seasonal thing .

So you have to supplement with feed . The cost of inputs , of feed and so on , skyrockets . Every year it goes up . Every year it goes up , and in the end , you are only alive because of the subsidy . Livestock management was also much more dependent on veterinary products . The animals were kept indoors more often , and we did deworming , vaccinations , and basically everything the veterinarians recommended .

The issue of keeping the livestock enclosed or stalled longer inevitably leads to diseases and intensive use of veterinary products . The herd starts to have problems , of course . It starts to have many types of problems , diarrhea , a whole host of them , and you look for the solution in veterinary products .

The soil suffers , because we have shallow soil , poor soil with a slope . The moment you introduce intensive agricultural tillage , you lose fertile soil at an incredible rate without even realizing it ; gullies open up , and the problem you see is that you have to close them because you pass through there with the tractor and hit a bump , and you don't realize that what you are losing is your heritage .

Little by little , the soil starts giving you less yield . At first , you believe the good harvest is due to chemical fertilizer , but then you realize that by applying it , you aren't really doing anything ; you've actually been living off the organic matter that the soil had , consuming that reservoir of life as if it were just a consumable , and once you've exhausted it , no matter how much fertilizer you add , you can't achieve the harvests you had at the

beginning . Another effect is that the fungi disappear , the earthworms disappear . In the beginning , when we were turning over the plot with the plow , you would have a bunch of birds following behind , eating worms and so on . After a few years , there isn't even a bird ; the soil is dying , losing more and more life , with fewer and fewer bugs .

Then , also with the massive deworming we did to the herd , it turns out you're killing all the coprophages , all the beetles that help you spread the manure and bury it . Well , all of that dies off with the ivermectins . It's a massacre of all the biodiversity and all the life that the soil had . You lose it little by little .

There are fewer and fewer birds , fewer bird songs . Everything is fading away and you don't even notice because since it happens day by day , it's such a subtle thing , you don't realize it until someone tells you . Someone comes along and says , " Don't you realize you've lost the fertile soil , that you've lost the diversity , that you have no worms , that you have no life ?

" You're so happy , thinking you were doing a damn good job . We were looking for alternatives and we discovered holistic management and met Savory ; we went to specific holistic management courses and trained in that , and for us , it was a discovery . That's when we came into contact with grazing planning and things we implemented along with Keyline design .

The most powerful thing was holistic management , and we have clearly seen that fertility , life , and soil regeneration follow good livestock management and good grazing . With livestock , not only do you not deplete the soil or harm it , but you actually favor it in a brutal way . The moment you start moving the cattle , you start moving the herd , you unify it and you start respecting rest periods , the land responds ; life starts appearing again , you start

to see : mushrooms return , fungi return , earthworms return , birds return . Through these holistic management courses , we came into contact with a group of people who had similar concerns . We are part of the Alej principle , we are a demonstration farm . It is a great backing and support to have people like us , ranchers , technicians , and veterinarians who share the same concern for life and for changing the industrial model .

And we also have the Savory Institute behind us , which is international support . So there is a lot of research behind this , and for us to be part of this system or this team is a great satisfaction . When we began implementing holistic management , the first thing we considered was defining our goal , our holistic context .

Well , it was difficult for us — well , it’s difficult for everyone , right ? But it was difficult for us because you have to think about where you want to go , what is important , and what is secondary . It’s a bit hard , and you never have time to stop and think about where you want to go , what you want your farm to look like in 50 years , how you would like to leave it to those who come after ; but it is work that gives you perspective , makes you see what

is important and what is not , and it takes you out of the day-to-day , out of daily tasks , and focuses you on what is truly important . So , defining our holistic context gave us a vision that you don't see when you are dragged along by daily tasks . So it is an important task . It is important to stop and see where you want to go and then adapt your daily tasks to those important goals , to that context , to that which you want to achieve .

Yes , in addition to the holistic goal or holistic context , financial planning also gives you perspective on the money you have , and for us , it was a revolution to pour resources into wealth-generating expenses . Uh , we come from a model where your resources are invested in inputs , in fertilizer , in cattle feed , and with holistic management we began to change that focus to say , " No , we are going to spend money on something that pays off .

" And in our case , it's fencing , reducing the size of the fences , and decreasing fertilizer costs which , well , as of today are practically zero . And well , let me tell you , regarding feed , it’s less and less because those resources return income to you , they return pasture ; we have more and more pasture .

So , the herd needs less feed . That's how it is . So , you see that with financial planning , and year by year we see how expenses are changing and how income is increasing , mostly due to the decrease in expenses . The biggest investments we make in financial planning are in fencing , where we’ve gone from having 25 - hectare fences to having eight , and each year they keep getting smaller .

In some places , we’re already at four or between four and five hectares in Zapatera , and these are expenses that scare you a bit at first , but the resource comes from the disappearance of spending on feed and fertilizers . So , you invest those resources there and you see how those plots respond more and more , because with the cattle concentrated and by respecting the rest periods , it gives you more grass .

It gives you more grass . If it rains , if you have good years , you go much faster and recover the investment sooner , but you aren't talking about huge timeframes ; you're talking about two or three years to recover . Of course , it depends on how fast you want to go to recover the cost of the fences and then also the issue of the ponds that goes with it ; you need water , and in Zapatera we opted for a piping system and in Mundo Nuevo more for ponds .

We have built a lot of ponds there , and it gives you peace of mind knowing that these investments are long-term , they are forever . When you buy feed , when you buy fertilizer , the next year you have to make that expense all over again . When you build a fence , that stays there for 20 , 30 , 40 years .

And a pond , the same . Besides the ponds , when you are improving soil hydration , providing moisture , and supplying water not only to your livestock but also to the wildlife , you are creating microclimates on your farm that are improving the ecosystem and the entire environment . So , you are spending resources , you are spending money on something you are seeing , hearing , and feeling , which is improving your farm .

We have planned our land use by taking the topography into account to make the most of all the water that falls on us . We are in an area with very low rainfall , and we cannot afford to lose a single drop of water . With the previous agricultural management , we plowed in long , straight furrows ; the moment it rained , the water would run off , but with the keyline hydrological design , we move water from the valley to the slopes , and the infiltration is

enormous . We also design ponds and channels , and based on those ponds and channels , we set up our fencing , so it’s all part of a land plan that is being implemented little by little . Logically , you can't do everything in the first year , but since you take available resources into account , you apply it gradually , and it is a holistic system .

The grazing plan is a bit like the holistic context : you never find the time , but it gives you many clues and a great global idea of the pasture you have . Although it is an estimate and gets adjusted , you refine it more every year , perfecting it year by year ; you learn from the things you missed in the previous grazing plan , and in a way , you keep learning .

Our grazing plan has infinite variables , but we are very much conditioned by the lambing seasons . The plan on paper, and what we said about holistic financial planning, is that expenses are classified differently than in traditional methods.

In traditional microeconomic analysis, for example, expenses are considered versus investments. When investments last more than one fiscal year, expenses are considered when they are consumed within the fiscal year. We obtain fixed expenses and variable expenses. Fixed expenses are structural expenses, permanent expenses that are not dependent on the volume produced.

Variable expenses do vary with the volume produced. Well, in holistic financial planning, we classify expenses into three groups, three categories: wealth-generating expenses are those that have the capacity to change, generate new wealth among social or biological capital, resolve a bottleneck, or increase income above current income.

Thus, an expense that generates wealth this year might be maintenance next year because we already made the expenditure. Inescapable expenses are, as their name indicates, expenses that respond to legal or moral obligations, so there is no way to negotiate these expenses. That is, I cannot reduce these expenses.

Imagine, for example, a lease agreement or the maintenance of the company's infrastructure. Family matters are non-negotiable because they involve a legal or moral obligation, like taxes. Then there's everything that isn't wealth-generating or unavoidable—maintenance, care, love, or maintenance expenses.
